articles.title: South Korea: Medication Abortion Rules Too Restrictive
articles.description: Click to expand Image A box of Mifepristone combined with Misoprostol tablets, May 2026. © 2026 Soumyabrata Roy/NurPhoto via AP Photo (Tokyo) – A South Korean government proposal would allow medication abortion in South Korea in 2027, but overly restrictive regulations will continue to impair the right of women and girls to safe and affordable abortion services, Human Rights Watch said today. National Assembly members have questioned government officials about the plan during a parliamentary audit. Seven years after South Korea’s Constitutional Court ruled the country’s decades-long abortion ban unconstitutional, effectively decriminalizing abortion and ordering legal reform by the end of 2020, the government has yet to amend the law to explicitly guarantee abortion rights. The government’s new proposal would finally establish a regulatory framework for medication abortion using Mifegymiso, a combination of Misoprostol and Mifepristone recognized by the World Health Organization (WHO) as the safest and most effective regimen. But access to the medication will remain unnecessarily impaired. “Allowing use of abortion pills is an important step, but South Korean lawmakers need to ensure that regulations aren’t so restrictive that abortions are inaccessible and unaffordable,” said Susanne Bergsten, acting women’s rights research assistant at Human Rights Watch. “Access to safe abortion is essential to protecting the autonomy, health, and rights of women and girls.” The draft rules would, for the first two years, permit medication abortions only up to nine weeks of pregnancy and specify that only doctors in large hospitals can prescribe and dispense the medication. If no side effects are found, it would likely be distributed more widely after the trial period. These restrictions are inconsistent with best practices, which endorse use of these medications up to 12 weeks, and with WHO recommendations that a broad range of health workers be authorized to manage medical abortion. Blocking many qualified providers from prescribing and dispensing the medication could hinder patients from receiving timely and critical care. Denying or delaying abortion access violates the rights to life, health, privacy, and freedom from discrimination. Mifepristone is approved by around 100 countries worldwide, and has been used safely in France and China for nearly 40 years. Major complications requiring hospitalization following medication abortion are very rare and occur in less than 1 percent of cases. The WHO also recommends telemedecine models of medical abortion care, in which prescriptions can be sent directly to pharmacies for self-administration at home. It considers this approach as safe for pregnancies of up to 12 weeks, provided the pregnant person has “accurate information, quality medicines and support from a trained health worker (if she needs or wants it during the process).” South Korea is obligated under international human rights law to ensure that all women and girls in the country can readily access timely, affordable, and safe abortion services. To meet these obligations, the National Assembly urgently needs to enact legislation that clarifies the decriminalization of abortion, and amends South Korea’s Mother and Child Health Act to ensure that the rights of pregnant people are protected in all areas relevant to safe abortion care, including health care, counseling, and support services. Abortions should be available at a pregnant person’s request, without requirements for parental or partner consent, notification or involvement, or accompaniment for adolescents or women with disabilities. Lawmakers should ensure that abortion services are covered by the National Health Insurance plan, to avoid costs becoming a barrier that prevents people from accessing abortion services. The government currently operates a crisis counseling system under the Special Act on Crisis Pregnancy and Protected Childbirth, enacted in 2023 for women and girls with unwanted or unintended pregnancies. However, the system has been criticized for not providing neutral advice and failing to provide adequate information about abortion, delaying access to abortion care. The law, which was intended to address unregistered births, also failed to introduce a comprehensive framework to ensure that all women in South Korea can register their child's birth, access pre- and postnatal care, receive financial support and services, and be free from the stigma and discrimination often faced by single mothers. The government should take genuine measures to support all pregnant people, whether they choose to continue or terminate a pregnancy by ensuring access to healthcare services throughout their pregnancy, at childbirth, and for childcare support. The government should also improve support and access to information for women and girls experiencing unintended or unwanted pregnancies. A 2023 report by Moimnet (Network to Assure Rights for Safe Abortion for All) found that many people face difficulties obtaining reliable abortion information. The government should provide unbiased information about reproductive health and abortion care, and ensure that schools deliver comprehensive, age-appropriate sexuality education. People seeking abortions should be able to make informed and autonomous decisions with support from healthcare providers who offer unbiased and respectful care. “South Korea’s National Assembly should swiftly align abortion legislation with international human rights standards to protect patients and providers,” Bergsten said. “Without safe and affordable access to abortion services, women and girls cannot fully experience their autonomy and reproductive rights.”

articles.title: What’s really fueling the recent generosity boom
articles.description: Generosity is in the air, or so it would seem. The Trump administration recently mailed a round of $500 checks to almost a million users of Healthcare.gov. The AI rivals OpenAI and Anthropic have promised to share their (eventual) wealth with the public beyond investors, and Anthropic this week got a bit more specific, proposing a Public Benefit Fund pegged at 5% of the company’s overall value. And never to be outdone, Elon Musk promptly pledged to give “every kid in America” a share in SpaceX. What explains the abrupt rise of these largesse Olympics among some of our most powerful institutions? Presumably there’s actual generosity involved. But let’s face it: Each of these schemes doubles as reputational marketing. Naturally, the details vary. The government checks are the most straightforward. They are accompanied by a letter ostensibly from President Trump, attacking Democrats and promising to lower healthcare costs. If that’s not a blatant enough pitch to vote Republican in the midterm election, the White House has also promised a $5,000 “Trump dividend” cash payment to every adult U.S. citizen—but only if the GOP keeps control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. So far this blunt generosity-as-persuasion approach doesn’t seem wildly effective; voters appear highly skeptical that the Trump dividend will materialize under any circumstances. For the artificial intelligence giants, the scenario is more nuanced. For some time now, the enormous promises attached to the technology have been accompanied by warnings of enormous risks. These range from taking our jobs to energy hog data centers to the more sci-fi-ish possibilities of wiping out humanity. The leaders of some of these companies haven’t exactly been shy about darker potentials—to the point that some have accused them of practicing a kind of doomsday marketing. Finding some way to share a portion of whatever wealth AI creates might take the edge off at least some of the doomer worries. It also gives the companies a happier talking point that spotlights their potential impact on life, and the stock market in particular. Anthropic now says it will commit 5% of its shares to the creation of the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a limited liability corporation. Anthropic is reportedly eyeing an IPO, and was valued recently at nearly $1 trillion, so this new entity would not be trivial. The company doesn’t yet have concrete plans for the fund, but has floated labor market impacts as a potential focus. This approach has some precedents. Salesforce, Google, and others have set aside corporate equity for social purposes, and Mark Zuckerberg and Priscilla Chan have pledged most of their Meta shares toward a philanthropic LLC. But at this stage, at least, Anthropic’s version strikes some as more performative than transparent or generous. “Trying,” as one critic put it, “to curry public favor.” Of course they are trying to curry public favor! That’s the point: Just as political actors depend on public sentiment leaning their way, so do high-profile businesses whose mission entails a plan to reshape the society. Which brings us to Musk, who has become both a political figure as well as an aspiring society-shaping tech entrepreneur. Musk’s announcement was in part responding directly to Anthropic, criticizing its plan for funneling equity through a vehicle it ultimately controls, and arguing for giving shares directly to the public. Granting one share apiece to “every kid” in America would involve about 73 million people under 18, adding up to about $11 billion in stock. (Musk is worth upwards of $900 billion, depending on market conditions.) He would apparently use the government’s new so-called “Trump accounts” to manage the giveaway. Gwynne Shotwell, president of SpaceX, and her husband earlier promised a share apiece to 2 million American children in the program, and Michael and Susan Dell have pledged $6.25 billion from their own foundation to help seed the program. Many details of Musk’s gift aren’t clear—but the message is hard to miss. His generosity is personal, record-setting, unambiguous, and, not incidentally, smarter than Anthropic’s (in Musk’s view). Musk has long been image conscious, and has more reason than ever to try to burnish his public persona. Aside from being the world’s richest man, he’s attracted increasing attention to his politics and geopolitical influence, from spending millions in campaign contributions on midterm races to accusations that his SpaceX throttled Ukraine’s access to the vital Starshield service associated with the company’s Starlink satellite network. It makes sense that a nonelected individual with global influence would want to project benevolence from time to time. And there’s something almost flex-like in handing out shares to every child in the country; even Musk’s philanthropy is a little intimidating. To be clear, generosity is a positive force, and there’s no call to be cynical. A gift does not become economically meaningless because it generates good publicity, including warm fuzzies toward the giver. But then again, the image payoff that comes with the announcement of generosity is immediate. What ultimately matters is when—or even whether—the actual generosity manifests.
